Sicilian Defense: 1.e4 c5. Named for its resemblance to a defensive pattern noted by Sicilian analysts as early as the 1600s. Black immediately fights for the center asymmetrically rather than mirroring White, which usually produces sharp, unbalanced, tactical positions where both sides play for a win. It's the single most popular reply to 1.e4 at every level from club to World Championship, and is considered fully sound — arguably Black's most ambitious option, though it demands a lot of theoretical knowledge.
Ruy Lopez: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5. Named after Ruy López de Segura, a 16th-century Spanish priest who wrote an early analysis of it (it's also called the Spanish Game). White develops naturally while eyeing the knight defending Black's e5-pawn. It's patient and positional rather than a quick attack — pressure builds slowly — and it's one of the most respected, deeply analyzed openings in chess, a mainstay of top-level play for well over a century.
French Defense: 1.e4 e6. Named simply for its long association with French players/analysts (it was championed in an 1834 correspondence match by Paris against London). Black accepts a slightly cramped position temporarily in exchange for a solid pawn structure and a clear plan to strike back at White's center later with ...c5 or ...f6. Solid and strategically rich rather than aggressive out of the gate; well regarded and reliable, if sometimes criticized for Black's initially passive-looking bishop.
Queen's Gambit Declined: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6. Black doesn't take the c4-pawn, instead reinforcing the center — the point being that grabbing the pawn (Queen's Gambit Accepted) often just hands White easy development to win it back. A classical, positional battleground rather than sharp; it's one of the most respected and thoroughly-tested defenses in existence, used at the very highest level for well over a century.
Italian Game: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4. Called Italian for its heavy development and analysis by Italian players from the 1500s–1600s onward (also known as Giuoco Piano, Italian for "quiet game" — somewhat ironic since sharp lines like the Evans Gambit branch from it). Aims the bishop straight at Black's weak f7-square for quick, natural development. Considered sound and flexible — can be played quietly or very aggressively depending on the sub-variation — and is popular at every level, including as a favorite modern practical weapon.
English Opening: 1.c4. Named after English champion Howard Staunton, who favored it in the 1843 match that helped popularize it. A flank opening: White delays occupying the center with pawns and instead controls it from the sides, often transposing into other structures. Flexible and positional rather than forcing; considered a very sound, respected choice at all levels, popular as a way to sidestep heavily-analyzed 1.e4/1.d4 theory.
King's Gambit Accepted: 1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4. White sacrifices the f-pawn immediately to rip open the center and the f-file for a fast attack — one of the oldest recorded openings, a favorite of the Romantic 19th-century era of chess. Very aggressive and tactical. It's sound enough to be playable, but modern engine-level defense has shown Black can often neutralize the attack with precise play, so it's less common at the top today than in chess's early history, though still a sharp practical weapon.
King's Indian Defense: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6, with ...Bg7 and ...d6. Part of the "Indian" family (see the Indian Defense entry below for the name's origin). Black cedes the center to White early, then plans a kingside fianchetto and a later pawn storm/piece attack against it. Famous for producing sharp, opposite-wing attacking races rather than quiet maneuvering; a longtime favorite of aggressive players (Kasparov most famously) and considered fully sound at the highest level.
Caro-Kann Defense: 1.e4 c6. Named after 19th-century analysts Horatio Caro and Marcus Kann, who first wrote it up. Black prepares ...d5 without blocking in the queen's bishop the way the French Defense does. Solid and resilient rather than flashy — a classic "steady, not sharp" choice — and it has a strong reputation as one of Black's most reliable defenses against 1.e4.
Nimzo-Indian Defense: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4. Named after Aron Nimzowitsch, the hypermodern theorist who popularized it — Black pins White's knight and often accepts doubled pawns in exchange for the bishop pair and long-term structural pressure. Strategically rich rather than immediately aggressive; considered one of the most reliable and respected defenses to 1.d4 at every level, including the very top.
Queen's Pawn Game: 1.d4 d5 (or similar) without either side committing to a specific named system yet. A broad, flexible label for closed, positional Queen's-pawn structures rather than a single strategy — it usually transposes into something more specific (Queen's Gambit, Colle System, London System, etc.) a move or two later. Generally solid and low-risk for both sides.
Dutch Defense: 1.d4 f5. Named for early Dutch analysis and enthusiasm for the line. Black stakes an immediate, somewhat provocative claim on the kingside/center with an early ...f5, aiming for active, often aggressive piece play rather than a slow buildup. It has a reputation as a slightly riskier, more combative choice than mainstream Indian defenses, but is fully playable and has had strong practitioners at top level.
Semi-Slav Defense: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 e6 — a hybrid of the Slav and Queen's Gambit Declined move orders. Extremely deeply analyzed and known for producing some of the sharpest, most theoretical positions in all of chess (the Meran and Botvinnik variations especially). Considered very sound and is a top-level mainstay, though it demands serious opening preparation.
Benoni Defense: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5, often followed by ...cxd4 and ...e6/...g6. Named from the Hebrew for "son of sorrow" (from an old opening-theory book title) — fittingly, Black accepts a somewhat cramped structure with a backward d-pawn in exchange for active piece play and pressure on White's center. Aggressive and imbalanced rather than solid; considered playable and dangerous in the right hands, though objectively slightly favoring White with precise play.
Grünfeld Defense: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5. Named after Austrian grandmaster Ernst Grünfeld, who introduced it in the 1920s. Black deliberately lets White build a big pawn center, then attacks it immediately with pieces — a hypermodern idea. Dynamic and sharp rather than passive; long considered one of the most reputable, fully sound defenses to 1.d4, used by World Champions.
Queen's Gambit Accepted: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4. Black grabs the offered pawn — but it's not really a true gambit in practice, since White almost always regains the pawn with active development. Leads to open, somewhat freer piece play for both sides compared to the Declined lines. Solid and well-respected, if slightly less common than the Declined main line.
Alekhine Defense: 1.e4 Nf6. Named after World Champion Alexander Alekhine, who introduced it in 1921. A provocative, hypermodern idea: Black invites White to chase the knight around with pawns and build a big center, planning to undermine it later. Sharp and somewhat risky for Black if White plays energetically, but fully playable and a good surprise weapon; it directly tempts White into overextending.
Indian Defense: 1.d4 Nf6 — the general family name (see the King's Indian, Nimzo-Indian, Queen's Indian, etc. for its specific branches). The name traces to 19th-century Indian player Moheschunder Bannerjee, whose flexible, fianchetto-based games (recorded by the Scottish master John Cochrane in Calcutta) looked strikingly different from the classical European style of the time and got labeled "Indian." Not aggressive by itself — it's a patient, hypermodern choice that delays central pawn commitments — but it's the gateway into some of the most respected defenses in all of chess.
King's Gambit Declined: 1.e4 e5 2.f4, and Black doesn't take on f4 (often 2...Bc4 or 2...d6). A calmer response to White's aggressive pawn sacrifice, keeping the position more solid rather than inviting the sharp complications of the Accepted lines. Considered a safe, sound way to meet the King's Gambit without wading into its deepest theory.
Scotch Game: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4. Named after an 1824 correspondence match between the Edinburgh and London chess clubs. White opens the center immediately rather than developing slowly. Direct and somewhat sharper than the main Ruy Lopez lines; fell out of top-level fashion for a while but was revived successfully (notably by Kasparov in the 1990s) and is considered fully sound.
Queen's Indian Defense: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6. Black fianchettoes the queen's bishop to control the long diagonal and the key e4-square, rather than grabbing space. Quiet and highly solid rather than aggressive — often described as one of Black's most reliable, risk-averse defenses to 1.d4 — and it's been a staple at World Championship level.
Slav Defense: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6. Black defends the d5-pawn without blocking in the queen's bishop, unlike the Queen's Gambit Declined. Solid and resilient; considered one of the most trustworthy, well-tested defenses to the Queen's Gambit at every level, valued for its structural soundness.
Petrov's Defense: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6. Also called the Russian Defense/Petroff, after 19th-century Russian master Alexander Petrov. Black mirrors White's development rather than defending the e5-pawn directly, aiming to simplify into a very safe, symmetrical position. Known as an extremely solid, drawish-leaning choice — a common "safe equalizer" at the top level when a player just wants a level position with Black.
Four Knights Game: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6. Both sides develop knights before anything else — one of the oldest, most classical development schemes in chess. Quiet and solid rather than sharp; it has a reputation as a slightly drawish, symmetrical opening, though modern sidelines have added some fresh venom to it.
Zukertort Opening: 1.Nf3. Named after 19th-century master Johannes Zukertort. A flexible move that avoids committing to a pawn structure immediately and can transpose into almost anything (Réti, English, Queen's Pawn systems). Not aggressive by itself — it's a flexible, transpositional choice — and is considered very safe and sound.
Scandinavian Defense: 1.e4 d5. Black strikes at the center immediately, offering to trade off e4/d5 tension right away rather than build up slowly (it's also called the Center Counter Defense). Considered fairly solid and low-theory compared to sharper 1.e4 replies, making it a popular practical choice for players who want a simple, reliable structure without memorizing huge amounts of theory.
Philidor Defense: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6. Named after 18th-century French master François-André Danican Philidor, who famously argued pawns were "the soul of chess" and championed solid pawn play over quick piece attacks. Passive-looking but sturdy; considered a bit passive and slightly worse for Black with precise play, so it's more of a solid, low-risk choice than a fighting try for a win.
Réti Opening: 1.Nf3 (followed by c4/g3 setups). Named after Richard Réti, one of the hypermodern school's leading theorists in the 1920s, who argued the center could be controlled from a distance with pieces rather than occupied with pawns immediately. Flexible and positional rather than aggressive; a very well-respected, sound flank opening at every level.
Nimzowitsch Defense: 1.e4 Nb8-c6 (i.e. 1.e4 Nc6). Named after Aron Nimzowitsch, in the same hypermodern spirit as his more famous Nimzo-Indian — Black develops a piece rather than a pawn and stays flexible about the center. Somewhat offbeat and less theoretically dense than mainstream 1.e4 replies; playable and a good surprise weapon rather than a top-tier main line.
Bishop's Opening: 1.e4 e5 2.Bc4. One of the oldest recorded openings, predating modern opening theory. Aims the bishop at f7 immediately, often transposing into Italian Game or King's Gambit-like structures. Not especially sharp on its own, but flexible, and it's had a resurgence as a way to dodge well-prepared Petrov/Berlin defenses.
Vienna Game: 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3. Named after the Austrian Vienna school of players in the late 1800s. Keeps options open for either a quiet developing game or a sharp f4 pawn-storm attack (the Vienna Gambit). Flexible in character — can be played gently or aggressively — and is considered a solid, respectable, if slightly less common alternative to 3.Nf3 lines.
Modern Defense: 1.e4 g6 (or 1.d4 g6). Black fianchettoes the king's bishop immediately without committing central pawns, staying maximally flexible about how to meet White's setup. Hypermodern and somewhat provocative; playable at a high level but considered to require careful, precise handling since Black gives White a free hand in the center for a while.
King's Pawn Game: 1.e4, before Black's reply narrows things into a specific named defense. The most classical, most heavily analyzed first move in chess, fighting for the center and freeing both the king's bishop and queen immediately. Neither inherently aggressive nor passive — its character is entirely defined by what follows.
Van Geet Opening: 1.Nc3. Named after Dutch player Dick van Geet, who championed it as a flexible, offbeat try. Keeps the position unusual and avoids mainstream theory rather than fighting for a big central advantage. Considered a sound if unambitious sideline, popular mainly as a practical surprise weapon.
Catalan Opening: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 — a Queen's Gambit structure with White's king's bishop fianchettoed instead of developed normally. Named for a 1929 tournament held in Barcelona, Catalonia. Quietly strategic rather than sharp: White presses on the long diagonal and against Black's queenside for a long time. Extremely well-respected at the very highest level — a favorite of many recent World Champions for its low-risk, long-term pressure.
Bird Opening: 1.f4. Named after 19th-century English master Henry Bird. A flank opening that stakes out kingside space early, sometimes transposing into Dutch Defense-like structures with colors reversed. Somewhat provocative and slightly risky (it weakens White's own king position a touch) but fully playable as a surprise weapon.
Pirc Defense: 1.e4 d6 (with ...Nf6, ...g6 to follow). Named after Slovenian grandmaster Vasja Pirc. Black lets White build a full pawn center and plans to attack it later with pieces, similar in spirit to the King's Indian but a tempo down. Hypermodern and somewhat provocative — considered playable and respectable, if objectively a bit more comfortable for White than the fully mainstream defenses.
Tarrasch Defense: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 c5. Named after Siegbert Tarrasch, a leading 19th/20th-century theorist. Black accepts an isolated queen's pawn later in exchange for active, free piece play — a deliberate trade of a small structural weakness for dynamism. A long-respected, sound choice, championed at world level by players like Kasparov and Kramnik.
Polish Opening: 1.b4. Also called the Sokolsky Opening or Orangutan. A flank opening grabbing queenside space immediately rather than fighting for the center directly. Considered slightly offbeat and not fully equalizing against best defense, but a reasonable practical surprise choice at club level.
Blackmar-Diemer Gambit Accepted: 1.d4 d5 2.e4 dxe4 (and White continues with f3/Nc3 to regain the pawn). A genuine gambit: White sacrifices a pawn early for fast, active piece development and open lines toward Black's king. Sharp and aggressive by design, popular among attacking club players, though considered objectively slightly dubious against precise defense at higher levels.
Bogo-Indian Defense: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+. Named after grandmaster Efim Bogoljubov. A calmer cousin of the Nimzo-Indian, played when White hasn't yet developed the knight to c3. Solid and slightly quieter than the Nimzo-Indian; considered a sound, if modest, way for Black to avoid deep main-line theory.
Grob Opening: 1.g4. Named after Swiss player Henri Grob, who championed it despite (or because of) its reputation as objectively dubious — it weakens White's own kingside for very little central gain. Considered more of a trick/surprise weapon than a sound main strategy, though it can be effective against unprepared opponents.
Hungarian Opening: 1.g3. A quiet flank opening fianchettoing the king's bishop before committing to a central plan, keeping maximum flexibility. Calm and positional rather than aggressive; considered fully sound, if modest in ambition, similar in spirit to the Réti/English family.
King's Indian Attack: A White setup (g3, Bg2, Nf3, O-O, d3/e4) that mirrors King's Indian Defense ideas with colors reversed, playable against almost anything Black does. Flexible and strategically patient rather than immediately sharp, building toward a kingside attack later; well-regarded as a reliable, easy-to-learn system, notably used by Bobby Fischer.
Nimzo-Larsen Attack: 1.b3. Named for Aron Nimzowitsch's ideas and popularized by Bent Larsen. White fianchettoes the queen's bishop immediately to control the long diagonal and center from a distance rather than occupy it with pawns. Flexible, hypermodern, and considered a fully sound, if quieter, alternative to main-line first moves.
Center Game: 1.e4 e5 2.d4. White opens the center immediately, often exchanging queens early after 2...exd4 3.Qxd4. Direct rather than sharp in the attacking sense — early queen development can cost time — considered playable but slightly old-fashioned and less ambitious than the Scotch Game, which delays the queen's development.
Latvian Gambit: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5. Black sacrifices structural safety very early for fast piece activity and open lines toward White's king. One of the sharpest, riskiest replies to 2.Nf3 — considered objectively dubious with best play but dangerous in practice, since it leads to unusual positions few opponents have studied deeply.
Ponziani Opening: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3. Named after 18th-century Italian player Domenico Lorenzo Ponziani. Prepares a big pawn center with d4 next rather than developing a piece. Solid and somewhat quiet; considered fully playable but a step below the main-line Ruy Lopez/Italian Game in popularity and theoretical weight.
Neo-Grünfeld Defense: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 d5 — a Grünfeld-style central strike against a fianchetto setup instead of Nc3. Shares the parent Grünfeld's dynamic, hypermodern character (see the Grünfeld Defense entry) in a slightly quieter structural form. Solid and well-regarded, if a touch less sharp than the main Grünfeld.
Old Indian Defense: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6. An earlier, quieter cousin of the King's Indian Defense, played before the fianchetto (...g6/...Bg7) systems became dominant. Solid and flexible rather than sharp; considered fully playable, though it's fallen out of top-level fashion in favor of its more actively-played descendants.
Trompowsky Attack: 1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5. Named after Brazilian master Octávio Trompowsky. White develops the bishop actively and provokes an early decision from Black's knight, sidestepping heavily-analyzed main lines. Aggressive in spirit and a popular surprise weapon; considered sound and has been played at the highest levels as a practical try.
Benko Gambit: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5. Named after grandmaster Pal Benko. Black sacrifices a queenside pawn permanently for long-term pressure down the open a- and b-files against White's queenside. A genuine, well-respected gambit — objectively somewhat compensated rather than fully equal, but very dangerous in practice and popular at every level.
London System: 1.d4 followed by Bf4, Nf3, e3, Bd3, Nbd2 — a flexible setup White can play against almost any Black response without memorizing deep, opponent-specific theory. Solid and low-risk rather than sharp; hugely popular at club level for its simplicity, and increasingly seen at the top level too as a reliable, low-theory weapon.
Danish Gambit: 1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3. White sacrifices one or even two pawns to open lines fast and get pieces on aggressive diagonals bearing down on Black's kingside. Very sharp and attacking by design; considered objectively dubious against accurate modern defense, but a dangerous practical weapon, especially at faster time controles.
Evans Gambit: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 — a branch of the Italian Game. Named after 19th-century sea captain William Davies Evans. White sacrifices a queenside pawn for rapid central expansion and development, aiming straight at Black's king. Aggressive and historically a favorite of attacking players (including a famous Kasparov revival in the 1990s); considered playable and dangerous, if not fully sound against best defense.
Budapest Gambit: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5. Black offers a pawn immediately to disrupt White's center and open lines for fast piece play, aiming for quick tactical chances rather than a long strategic game. Considered a sound surprise weapon rather than a main-line try — objectively a bit better for White with precise play, but tricky in practice.
Blackmar-Diemer Gambit: 1.d4 d5 2.e4 dxe4 3.Nc3 — White sacrifices a pawn (regained later, often via f3) purely for fast development and open lines toward Black's king. Very aggressive and attack-minded by design; has a devoted following among attacking club players, though it's generally considered slightly unsound against precise, well-prepared defense.
Vienna Gambit: A sharp branch of the Vienna Game (1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4) where White sacrifices a pawn to blast open the center and the f-file fast, in the same attacking spirit as the King's Gambit. Aggressive and tactical rather than positional; playable but demands accurate follow-up to justify the material given up.
Rat Defense: An irregular Black setup (an early ...d6 with flexible piece development, related to the Modern Defense) that avoids committing to a specific structure for as long as possible. Passive-looking and hypermodern rather than aggressive; considered playable but gives White a fairly free hand early on.
Kádas Opening: 1.h4 — an unusual first move grabbing kingside space immediately rather than fighting for the center. Named after the Hungarian player who experimented with it. Considered a fringe, largely unsound try at serious levels, more of a curiosity/surprise choice than a main strategy.
Englund Gambit: 1.d4 e5 — Black immediately offers a pawn to disrupt White's center rather than developing normally. A genuine, if objectively dubious, gambit: it can win a quick trap or two against unprepared opponents, but is not considered sound against accurate defense.
Owen Defense: 1.e4 b6 (or 1.d4 b6). Black fianchettoes the queen's bishop immediately, in the same hypermodern spirit as the Modern/Nimzo-Larsen family, without a specific named originator confirmed. Quiet and flexible rather than aggressive; a playable, low-theory sideline.
Richter-Veresov Attack: 1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 (heading for Bg5), named after German master Kurt Richter and Soviet player Gavriil Veresov. A flexible way to sidestep mainstream Queen's Gambit/Slav theory while still developing actively. Solid and somewhat quiet; considered a sound, practical alternative rather than a top-tier main line.
Ware Opening: 1.a4 — one of the more extreme flank tries, grabbing queenside space with essentially no other purpose this early. Named after 19th-century player Preston Ware, known for unorthodox openings. Considered largely unsound at any serious level, mostly a historical curiosity.
English Defense: 1.d4 (or 1.c4/1.Nf3) e6 followed by ...b6, fianchettoing the queen's bishop early against a queen's-pawn setup. Solid and flexible rather than sharp; a playable, somewhat offbeat choice that keeps Black's structure hard to attack directly.
Barnes Opening: 1.f3 — one of the weakest common first moves, blocking the king's knight's natural square for no compensating benefit. Named after 19th-century English player Thomas Wilson Barnes. Considered objectively poor and mostly of historical/curiosity interest rather than a real practical try.
Torre Attack: 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 followed by Bg5, named after Mexican master Carlos Torre Repetto. A flexible system aiming for solid development and central control without heavy memorization. Quiet and positional; considered a sound, practical choice at club level and above.
Lion Defense: A solid Black setup related to the Philidor Defense (an early ...d6, ...Nf6, ...Nbd7 structure) prioritizing a resilient pawn chain over quick piece activity. Passive-looking but sturdy; playable, if modest in ambition, similar in spirit to the Philidor.
Three Knights Opening: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3, before Black also develops a third knight (which would transpose to the Four Knights Game). Quiet, classical development; solid but not particularly ambitious, similar in character to the Four Knights Game.
Rubinstein Opening: A flexible reversed-Queen's-pawn setup associated with the ideas of World Championship contender Akiba Rubinstein, known for his deep positional understanding. Quiet and strategic rather than sharp; considered a sound, patient way to develop.
Van't Kruijs Opening: 1.e3 — a very modest, flexible first move that stakes no early claim on the center, keeping all options open. Named after 19th-century Dutch player Maarten van 't Kruijs. Considered playable but passive and unambitious compared to committing to the center directly.
Borg Defense: 1.e4 g5 (or 1.d4 g5) — a deliberately provocative, weakening pawn push very early, sometimes played as a joke on "Grob spelled backwards" (the Grob Opening played by Black). Considered objectively dubious and mostly a novelty/surprise choice rather than sound strategy.
Mieses Opening: 1.d3 — an extremely modest first move, similar in spirit to Van't Kruijs but on the queenside color, delaying all central commitment. Named after German master Jacques Mieses. Playable but passive; rarely seen above club level.
Sodium Attack: 1.e3, sometimes used as an alternate name for very quiet, flexible first-move setups (the "Sodium" name is informal chess-database slang rather than historical). Passive and non-committal in character; not a serious main try at higher levels.
Mikenas Defense: Associated with Lithuanian master Vladas Mikėnas, an early, somewhat provocative reply establishing a Black knight or pawn thrust before normal development. Sharp and offbeat rather than mainstream; a surprise weapon more than a deeply-trusted main line.
St. George Defense: 1.e4 a6 — Black makes a very slow, flexible waiting move instead of contesting the center. Named for a notable upset game played with it. Considered objectively passive and risky at serious levels, though it can throw an opponent out of preparation.
Elephant Gambit: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 — Black immediately offers a pawn to seize central space and open lines fast. A genuine but fairly obscure gambit; considered playable as a surprise try but not fully sound against precise defense.
Amar Opening: 1.Nh3 — a rare, deliberately offbeat first move developing the knight to the rim immediately. Named after French player Charles Amar. Considered objectively weak and mostly a novelty rather than a serious try.
Colle System: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 followed by e3, Bd3, and a later e4 break — named after Belgian master Edgard Colle. A simple, easy-to-learn setup White can play against many Black responses without deep memorization, similar in spirit to the London System. Solid and quiet; a long-standing, sound club-level favorite.
King's Pawn Opening: 1.e4 — an alternate label for the same King's Pawn Game family, before Black's reply narrows things further. See the King's Pawn Game entry: the most classical, heavily analyzed way to fight for the center.
Portuguese Opening: 1.e4 d5 2.Bb5+ — an early check that develops the bishop actively against the Scandinavian-style center strike. Aggressive-leaning and somewhat unusual; playable as a sideline rather than deep main theory.
King's Knight Opening: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 — the natural developing move before either side commits to a specific named system (Ruy Lopez, Italian Game, Scotch, etc. all branch from here). Neither aggressive nor passive on its own; its character is defined by what follows.
Rapport-Jobava System: A flexible d4/Nc3/Bf5-development scheme associated with modern grandmasters Richárd Rapport and Baadur Jobava, known for creative, engine-defying opening choices. Aggressive and offbeat rather than deeply theoretical; a popular modern surprise weapon at strong levels.
Blumenfeld Countergambit: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 b5 — Black sacrifices a pawn for a strong, mobile center and active piece play, in a similar spirit to the Benko Gambit. Aggressive and dynamic; considered a sound, if less common, fighting try for Black.
Anderssen's Opening: 1.a3 — an extremely modest, flexible first move that commits to almost nothing, named after 19th-century attacking legend Adolf Anderssen (better known for wild tactical brilliancies than this quiet try). Passive but perfectly playable as an offbeat, low-theory choice.
Clemenz Opening: 1.h3 — a very modest first move preparing quiet development while avoiding early theoretical fights. Considered passive and largely a curiosity rather than a serious try at any level of competition.
Formation: An ECO-database catch-all label for irregular early setups that don't fit a more specific named opening yet — the position's character depends entirely on what both sides do next rather than a defined plan.
Zukertort Defense: A Black setup echoing Johannes Zukertort's flexible, non-committal development ideas (see the Zukertort Opening) played from the Black side. Quiet and flexible rather than sharp; a sound, low-theory choice.
English Orangutan: A flank setup combining English Opening (1.c4) ideas with an early ...b5-style queenside pawn thrust, echoing the whimsically-named "Orangutan" (Polish Opening/1.b4) family. Offbeat and provocative rather than mainstream theory; mostly a surprise practical try.
Horwitz Defense: 1.d4 e6 — a flexible, modest reply keeping options open between French Defense and Queen's Gambit Declined-style structures. Named after 19th-century player Bernhard Horwitz. Solid and non-committal rather than sharp.
Kangaroo Defense: A Nimzo-Indian-adjacent Black setup (1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4, keeping the option of a later ...O-O or ...d5 open) named for its hopping, flexible move-order character. Quiet and strategic, similar in spirit to its Nimzo-Indian relative.
Polish Defense: 1.d4 b5 (or similar early ...b5 tries by Black) — an aggressive, space-grabbing queenside pawn push very early, mirroring the ambition of White's Polish Opening (1.b4) from the other side. Considered provocative and objectively a bit loose, more of a surprise weapon than sound main theory.
Slav Indian: A hybrid structure blending Slav Defense pawn play (...c6, ...d5) with Indian-style piece development (an early ...Nf6/fianchetto), staying flexible about which classical structure it ultimately resembles. Solid and strategic rather than sharp.
Amazon Attack: An aggressive early setup bringing the queen out actively alongside rapid piece development (the "Amazon" nickname historically refers to the queen's combined rook-and-bishop-like power). Sharp and somewhat risky since early queen moves invite tempo-gaining attacks; more of a surprise try than trusted theory.
Marienbad System: A flexible English Opening-related setup, associated with the 1925 Mariánské Lázně (Marienbad) tournament where it saw notable use. Positional and slow-building rather than sharp, in keeping with the English Opening family's general character.
Pseudo Queen's Indian Defense: A Black setup that resembles the Queen's Indian Defense's fianchetto plan but reaches it via a different move order that doesn't quite match the "real" line. Quiet and solid, sharing the genuine Queen's Indian's low-risk character (see that entry).
Mexican Defense: 1.d4 Nc6 (or similar), an unusual early knight development instead of a pawn move, echoing the Nimzowitsch Defense's hypermodern spirit from a different first move. Offbeat and low-theory; playable but not a mainstream try.
Carr Defense: An uncommon, sparsely documented Black defense; treat as an obscure sideline rather than established main theory — its character is best judged from the actual moves reached rather than a confident historical claim.
Goldsmith Defense: An uncommon, sparsely documented Black defense; treat as an obscure sideline rather than established main theory — its character is best judged from the actual moves reached rather than a confident historical claim.
Hippopotamus Defense: An extremely passive, slow Black setup (pawns on the third rank all across the board, pieces tucked behind them) named for how deep and defensive it looks. Very solid and hard to attack directly, but cedes a lot of space and initiative to White; a specialist, unusual choice rather than mainstream theory.
Ware Defense: 1.e4 a5 (echoing the same unusual flank-grabbing idea as the Ware Opening, played by Black). Considered objectively weak, mostly of historical/curiosity interest.
Amsterdam Attack: An uncommon named line associated with a tournament held in Amsterdam; treat as a rare sideline rather than established main theory.
Creepy Crawly Formation: A deliberately slow, space-conceding setup (pawns advanced just one square across a wide front, similar in spirit to the Hippopotamus Defense) that waits for the opponent to overextend before counterattacking. Very passive and patient rather than aggressive; a specialist choice, not mainstream theory.
Global Opening: A rarely-played irregular opening; treat as a curiosity rather than established main theory — its character is best judged from the actual moves reached.
Lasker Simul Special: A rare line associated with World Champion Emanuel Lasker's simultaneous exhibition games rather than serious tournament theory; treat as a historical curiosity.
Saragossa Opening: 1.c3 — a very modest first move preparing a slow d4 buildup without early commitment. Named after a tournament in Zaragoza, Spain. Passive but sound as a low-theory, flexible try.
Valencia Opening: A rare named line associated with a tournament in Valencia, Spain; treat as an uncommon sideline rather than established main theory.
Australian Defense: An uncommon, sparsely documented Black defense; treat as an obscure sideline rather than established main theory.
Montevideo Defense: A rare named line associated with a tournament in Montevideo, Uruguay; treat as an uncommon sideline rather than established main theory.
Zaire Defense: An uncommon, sparsely documented Black defense, its name associated with a tournament or game location; treat as an obscure sideline rather than established main theory.
Robatsch Defense: An alternate name for the Modern Defense (1...g6 fianchetto setups), after Austrian grandmaster Karl Robatsch, an early proponent. See the Modern Defense entry — hypermodern and flexible rather than aggressive.
Wade Defense: A flexible, Modern-Defense-adjacent Black setup associated with English international master Bob Wade. Quiet and hypermodern rather than sharp.
Basque Opening: A rare named line associated with the Basque Country region of Spain; treat as an uncommon sideline rather than established main theory.
Canard Opening: A rare, whimsically-named irregular opening ("canard" is French for "duck" — chess nicknames for odd openings are often playful); treat as a curiosity rather than established main theory.
Paleface Attack: A rare, informally-named irregular line; treat as a curiosity rather than established main theory.
Döry Defense: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Ne4 — an early, provocative knight incursion instead of normal development, named after Hungarian player Tibor Döry. Sharp and offbeat; considered objectively a bit loose, more of a surprise try than trusted theory.
Yusupov-Rubinstein System: A flexible Nimzo-Indian-adjacent setup associated with grandmaster Artur Yusupov, building on ideas from Akiba Rubinstein. Quiet and strategic, sharing the Nimzo-Indian family's solid reputation.
East Indian Defense: A flexible ...Nf6/...d6/...g6 move-order that can transpose into King's Indian or Old Indian structures without committing early. Hypermodern and patient, sharing that family's general character (see King's Indian Defense / Old Indian Defense).
Queen's Indian Accelerated: A faster move-order reaching Queen's Indian Defense-style structures (fianchettoing the queen's bishop) a tempo quicker than the main line. Shares the Queen's Indian's solid, low-risk reputation (see that entry).
Vulture Defense: An unusual early piece maneuver (a knight swooping toward the center in an irregular way) rather than standard development. Offbeat and sharp; a surprise try rather than trusted main theory.
Barnes Defense: 1.e4 f6 — an early, weakening pawn move that blocks the king's knight's best square, echoing Thomas Wilson Barnes's unorthodox style (see Barnes Opening). Considered objectively poor at serious levels.
Duras Gambit: A rare gambit line associated with Czech grandmaster Oldřich Duras, sacrificing material early for active piece play; treat as an uncommon sideline rather than deeply established theory.
Fried Fox Defense: A rare, colorfully-named Black defense; treat as a curiosity rather than established main theory.
Lemming Defense: A deliberately passive, self-effacing Black setup (the name plays on lemmings' reputation for blindly following) that cedes space and initiative early. Very passive; a novelty choice rather than sound main strategy.
Czech Defense: An alternate name associated with Caro-Kann/Slav-adjacent setups favored by Czech players historically; shares that family's solid, resilient character (see Caro-Kann Defense).
Bongcloud Attack: 1.e4 e5 2.Ke2 — an intentionally terrible move (walking the king out into the open for no reason) that became an internet-famous meme, popularized by streaming grandmasters like Hikaru Nakamura as a joke in casual/exhibition games. Objectively one of the worst possible moves in the position — played for laughs, not to win.
King's Gambit: 1.e4 e5 2.f4, before Black decides whether to accept or decline the offered pawn. See King's Gambit Accepted / Declined for how each response plays out — either way, one of the oldest and most aggressive openings in chess history.
Queen's Gambit: 1.d4 d5 2.c4, before Black decides whether to accept or decline the offered pawn. See Queen's Gambit Accepted / Declined for how each response plays out — a classical, deeply respected opening either way, sharper in spirit than its calm reputation suggests.
Queen's Pawn: 1.d4, before Black's reply narrows things into a specific named defense. See the Queen's Pawn Game entry — flexible and positional rather than forcing.
Pterodactyl Defense: A modern hypermodern setup combining an early ...g6 fianchetto with ...c5 and sometimes ...Qa5, striking at the center from multiple angles at once rather than occupying it (the name evokes the piece formation's swooping, angular shape). Sharp and provocative; a specialist, actively-played modern choice rather than deep classical theory.
Dresden Opening: A rare named line associated with a tournament held in Dresden, Germany; treat as an uncommon sideline rather than established main theory.
Gunderam Defense: A rare, sparsely documented Black defense; treat as an obscure sideline rather than established main theory.
Irish Gambit: 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 (offering a transposition to gambit-like play), a rare, lightly-documented sideline; treat as an uncommon try rather than established main theory.
